content: Peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase C (PPIC) is an enzyme in humans encoded by the PPIC gene located on chromosome 5. This enzyme belongs to the peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) family and catalyzes the cis-trans isomerization of proline imidic peptide bonds. This activity facilitates the proper folding and repair of proteins. PPIC is involved in numerous biological processes, including mitochondrial metabolism, apoptosis, redox regulation, and inflammation. It is also implicated in various pathological conditions such as ischemic reperfusion injury, AIDS, and cancer. Structurally, PPIC, like other cyclophilins, adopts a β-barrel configuration with a hydrophobic core. This β-barrel consists of eight anti-parallel β-strands capped by two α-helices at the top and bottom. The β-turns and loops within the strands contribute to the flexibility of the barrel. PPIC is composed of 212 amino acid residues and contains a hydrophobic, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-targeting sequence at its N-terminal. Its PPIase domain is homologous to PPIA and can be inhibited by cyclosporin A (CsA). The protein encoded by the PPIC gene is a member of the PPIase family, which catalyzes the cis-trans isomerization of proline imidic peptide bonds in oligopeptides, thereby accelerating protein folding. PPIases are highly conserved across eubacteria, eukaryotes, and some archaebacteria. The PPIase family is divided into three structurally distinct subfamilies: cyclophilin (CyP), FK506-binding protein (FKBP), and parvulin (Pvn). As a cyclophilin, PPIC binds cyclosporin A (CsA) and can be found intracellularly or secreted by cells. In eukaryotes, cyclophilins are ubiquitously localized across various cell and tissue types, with PPIC being highly expressed in the kidney. Cyclophilins, including PPIC, perform diverse functions beyond their PPIase and protein chaperone activities. These include roles in mitochondrial metabolism, apoptosis, immune responses, inflammation, and cell growth and proliferation. PPIC, along with PPIB, localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where it helps maintain redox homeostasis. Depletion of these cyclophilins results in hyperoxidation of the ER. In the brain, PPIC forms complexes with cyclophilin C-associated protein (CyCAP) to activate microglia and macrophage functions via the calcineurin/NFAT signaling pathway. Clinically, as a cyclophilin, PPIC binds the immunosuppressive drug CsA to form a CsA-cyclophilin complex. This complex targets calcineurin, inhibiting the signaling pathway responsible for T-cell activation. In cardiac myogenic cells, cyclophilins are activated by heat shock and hypoxia-reoxygenation and form complexes with heat shock proteins. This suggests a role for cyclophilins in cardioprotection during ischemia-reperfusion injury. Similarly, PPIC may provide neuroprotection by forming a complex with CyCAP to activate survival mechanisms and mitigate ischemic damage in the brain. Cyclophilin expression, including that of PPIC, is strongly correlated with cancer pathogenesis, although the precise mechanisms remain unclear. For example, studies have identified PPIC as a reliable marker of circulating tumor cells in epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC), suggesting its potential as a biomarker for cancer detection and treatment. PPIC has been shown to interact with several molecules, including: Cyclosporin A (CsA), Cyclophilin C-associated protein (CyCAP), Calcineurin, and NFATc1.
